title: Negative Weights & All-Pairs — Bellman-Ford & Floyd-Warshall
summary: Two problems Dijkstra can't solve: Bellman-Ford handles negative edge weights (and detects negative cycles) by relaxing every edge repeatedly; Floyd-Warshall computes every pair's shortest distance at once via a DP over intermediate nodes.

slides.markdown:
[dijkstra-shortest-paths](dijkstra-shortest-paths) covers single-source shortest paths when weights are non-negative — the common case, but not the only one. Two problems it can't handle: **negative edge weights** (Dijkstra's greedy proof depends on non-negativity) and **all-pairs distances** (computing every source's shortest paths at once, rather than one).

**Bellman-Ford** solves the first by relaxing every edge repeatedly, slower than Dijkstra but correct even with negative weights, and it can detect negative cycles as a byproduct. **Floyd-Warshall** solves the second with a dynamic program over intermediate nodes, trading Dijkstra's per-source efficiency for computing everything at once.

slides.sectionTitle: Bellman-Ford: relax every edge, V-1 times
slides.markdown:
Bellman-Ford's core loop is almost embarrassingly simple: relax **every** edge in the graph, in any order, and repeat that for **V-1** rounds total. A single relaxation of edge `(u, v, w)` checks if `dist[u] + w < dist[v]` and updates if so — the same relaxation Dijkstra does, just without any smart ordering.

Why V-1 rounds specifically: the shortest path between any two nodes in a graph with no negative cycle uses at most V-1 edges (a simple path can't repeat a node, so it can't have more than V-1 edges). Each full round of relaxing every edge guarantees that any shortest path's distance information propagates one edge further along its length — so after V-1 rounds, even the longest possible shortest path has been fully propagated.

slides.sectionTitle: The V-th round: detecting a negative cycle
slides.markdown:
If a graph has a **negative cycle** reachable from the source, "shortest path" is undefined for any node reachable through that cycle — you could loop the cycle indefinitely, making the path arbitrarily cheap each time around. Bellman-Ford detects this directly: run **one more round** (the V-th) of edge relaxation after the normal V-1. If *any* edge can still be relaxed in that extra round, a negative cycle exists somewhere reachable from the source.

The logic: V-1 rounds are provably enough to fully propagate any legitimate (cycle-free) shortest path. If something still improves on round V, that improvement isn't coming from a longer *simple* path — it's coming from looping a negative cycle, which is exactly the condition that makes the whole problem ill-defined.

slides.sectionTitle: Floyd-Warshall: routing through every intermediate node
slides.markdown:
Floyd-Warshall computes the shortest distance between **every pair** of nodes simultaneously, using a dynamic program indexed by an intermediate node `k`: `dist[i][j]` after considering intermediate nodes `1..k` is the shortest path from `i` to `j` that's allowed to route through any of nodes `1` through `k`.

The recurrence: `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])` — either the best path found so far without routing through `k`, or a path that goes through `k`. Running this for every `k` from 1 to V, in order, and updating the full matrix each time, ends with every pair's true shortest distance once all V nodes have been considered as potential intermediates.

slides.sectionTitle: The "via k" DP, building one intermediate at a time
slides.markdown:

Each stage's highlighted improvement should make concrete what "considering k as an intermediate" means: a pair (i, j) improves exactly when going i → k → j is cheaper than whatever direct or previously-discovered route existed before.

| | Dijkstra | Bellman-Ford | Floyd-Warshall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Handles negative weights? | No | Yes | Yes |
| Detects negative cycles? | No | Yes | Yes (negative diagonal entry) |
| Scope | Single source | Single source | All pairs |
| Complexity | O((V+E) log V) | O(V·E) | O(V³) |
| Best fit | Non-negative weights, one source, need speed | Negative weights possible, one source | Need every pair's distance, or V is small |

The honest way to pick: default to Dijkstra unless negative weights are possible (then Bellman-Ford) or you genuinely need all-pairs distances and V is small enough for O(V³) to be reasonable (then Floyd-Warshall) — reaching for Floyd-Warshall on a large sparse graph when you only need one source's distances is a common, avoidable overcomplication.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a negative cycle makes "shortest path" undefined
slides.markdown:
If a cycle's total edge weight is negative, walking around it repeatedly makes a path through it cheaper every additional lap — there's no lower bound. "What's the shortest path from A to B" has no well-defined answer if some path from A to B can route through that cycle, because you could always find a cheaper one by looping one more time.

This is a fundamentally different situation from a single negative edge with no cycle, which is perfectly fine to have a well-defined shortest path — the problem is specifically a cycle whose total weight sums to negative, not the mere presence of a negative number anywhere in the graph.

slides.sectionTitle: Stopping at V-1 rounds without the extra check
slides.markdown:
Implementing Bellman-Ford's V-1 relaxation rounds correctly but skipping the extra V-th round check means the algorithm will happily return distance values on a graph with a negative cycle — values that are simply wrong, since "shortest path" isn't well-defined there at all. The V-1 rounds alone only guarantee correct results **when no negative cycle exists**; without the extra check, there's no signal that the returned numbers are meaningless.

This is easy to skip because the first V-1 rounds "work" in the sense of producing *some* numbers — the bug is silent, not a crash, exactly the same failure shape as forgetting cycle detection in topological sort.

slides.sectionTitle: Reaching for Floyd-Warshall on a large sparse graph
slides.markdown:
Floyd-Warshall's O(V³) is fine when V is small (a few hundred nodes, easily) but becomes impractical fast — V = 5,000 already means 125 billion operations. On a large, sparse graph where you only need shortest paths from a handful of sources (not literally every pair), running repeated Dijkstra from each needed source (O(source count × (V+E) log V)) is typically far cheaper than one Floyd-Warshall pass over the whole graph.

The tell: if the problem only ever asks about a few sources, Floyd-Warshall is solving a much bigger problem (every pair) than what's actually needed, and paying for it in both time and O(V²) memory for the full distance matrix.
